title: Before 'America': The Wild Name Ideas the Founders Rejected
summary:
It's hard to imagine a world without the United States of America. But when the founding fathers were crafting a new nation in 1776, they had to decide what to call it—and they considered some surprising options.

Among the contenders were the United Colonies, the United Colonies of America, and even the United States of Alleghania (yes, really). The name "United" was crucial because the thirteen colonies knew they could only defeat the mighty British Army if they fought together. Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense urged unity, and Benjamin Franklin's famous 1754 woodcut of a snake chopped into pieces, captioned "Join, or Die," drove the point home.

On September 9, 1776, the Second Continental Congress officially ordered that the term "United Colonies" be replaced with "United States" in official documents. But here's a fascinating twist: in the Declaration of Independence, the word "united" appears with a lowercase "u"—"the thirteen united States of America." This wasn't a typo. As historian Edward J. Larson explains, the founders didn't see themselves as creating a single nation. They thought of it as a confederation of independent states, each retaining its own sovereignty. A Virginian identified as a Virginian first, not as an American.

The Articles of Confederation, adopted in 1781, reinforced this by declaring the confederacy would be called "The United States of America"—but also stating that each state kept its "sovereignty, freedom and independence." The central government was so weak it couldn't even levy taxes, leading to chaos by the mid-1780s.

That's why, in 1789, the Constitution replaced the Articles. It kept the name but shifted power to a stronger central government—and in its opening line, "We the People of the United States," the "U" in "United" is finally capitalized. That small change symbolized a big shift: from a loose alliance to a more unified nation. So next time you say the Pledge of Allegiance, remember the long, surprising journey of that name—and be glad they didn't choose Alleghania!
why_it_matters: The debate over how much power belongs to the national government and how much belongs to states did not end in 1789; it still shapes arguments over laws, schools, and rights today. Understanding that the phrase 'United States' once meant a loose alliance helps explain why American identity has always been a work in progress.

background_read: In 1776 the 13 British colonies in North America were fighting the Revolutionary War, but they did not yet have one clear, official name.
The Second Continental Congress (the delegates from the colonies who directed the war and acted as the new country's first government) had to settle on a name for the nation they hoped to create.

Thomas Paine, an English-born political writer whose pamphlet Common Sense argued for independence, and Benjamin Franklin, an American inventor and diplomat, both insisted that the colonies could only beat Britain by acting together.
The first official framework, the Articles of Confederation, created a loose league of sovereign states, but it proved too weak because Congress could not tax or force states to obey its decisions.
Between 1787 and 1790, the Constitution replaced that weak league with a stronger central government while still leaving many powers to the states.
That is why the name 'United States' is more than a label: it points to a lasting debate about the balance between national unity and state independence.

perspectives.description: Choosing 'United States' allowed the thirteen former colonies to keep their own identities while gaining strength through unity. The Constitution's stronger national government fixed many of the weaknesses that had made the early confederation unable to act.

perspectives.perspective: Negative / critical — critics of the early confederation
perspectives.description: The Articles of Confederation may sound ideal for state independence, but they created a government so weak it could not even collect taxes. States quarreled over money and borders, and the country nearly fell apart before the Constitution replaced the failed system.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical — historians of political language
perspectives.description: Capital letters and punctuation can carry political meaning. The lowercase 'u' in the Declaration and the capitalized 'U' in the Constitution are small clues to a major shift in how leaders imagined the nation: first as a league, later as one people.

Questions about states' rights, national standards, and shared identity are still alive. Knowing that the name 'United States' came from an argument between unity and independence can help young citizens make sense of current political conflicts rather than treating them as brand-new.
